idiom_name: GRDB belongsTo/hasMany derived from declared foreign keys
implementation_notes: GRDB takes the database's own foreign keys as the source of truth: the record holds the key value (var authorId: Int64?) and an association declared with belongsTo(Author.self) - plus hasMany(Book.self) on the other side - turns it into a request the database resolves, with including(optional: Book.author) joining the referenced row in one query. Core Data and SwiftData instead model the association as an object graph with no visible key, and Fluent uses @Parent/@Children. Hand-written mapping over SQLite.swift or the C API stays justified when another team owns the schema and no association layer is wanted.
pitfalls: GRDB explains associations from the declared foreign keys: if the SQLite constraint was never declared (or the table was hand-created), belongsTo falls back to a convention and then fails at query time.
Optionality must match the column - a non-optional Int64 decoding a NULL throws a decoding error, so nullable keys need Int64? and an optional association.
Records are value types: a mutation in one copy does not update others, so saving a stale copy can write back an outdated foreign key.
